title: How Long Should Time-Out Be?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin challenges the common advice that time-out should last as many minutes as a student's age, or an even shorter two to five minutes. His Smart Classroom Management plan recommends 12 to 15 minutes for kindergarten through third grade and 15 to 20 minutes for fourth through seventh, with eighth grade and up using a separate plan that has no time-out. He gives three reasons for longer time-outs: time to reflect and calm emotions, time to miss the class and so feel regret, and time to learn from the mistake through stronger accountability. He ties all three to a precondition, which is clear rules, consistency, and a classroom students enjoy belonging to. He finishes with the paradox that longer, more effective time-outs reduce future misbehavior, so students end up spending less total time in time-out over a school year.
points: Linsin recommends 12 to 15 minutes of time-out for K-3 and 15 to 20 minutes for grades 4 to 7, well beyond the common age-in-minutes rule.
Reflection only comes naturally when the rules are clear and the teacher follows the plan without adding a lecture or talking-to.
The effect depends on students wanting to return, so a classroom they enjoy being part of is what turns more time into deeper regret.
He suggests teachers watch for visible eagerness to return before letting a student leave time-out.
Because longer time-outs curb later misbehavior more effectively, he claims students will spend far less time in time-out across the school year.
quotes: The typical advice is that time-out should mirror in minutes the age of your students. So, for example, if a student is eight years old, then time-out should be eight minutes long.
Your students need time to calm their emotions, breathe a moment, and then begin reflecting on their misbehavior. This takes awhile.
If your rules are clear, you’re consistent, and you follow your plan to a tee rather than adding a lecture, talking-to, and the like, then effective reflection will come naturally.
What drives reflection and ultimately regret is when the student feels as if they’re missing something. They must want to return to their normal seat.
If this is the case, then more time equals deeper regret and greater desire to improve behavior.
The longer a student is able to sit with their mistake (within reason), the more fully they’ll learn from it.
They must be eager to return to the class they like being part of or time-out won’t be effective. By using longer time-outs, you’ll be able to see this eagerness on their face.
In this way, because longer time-outs are more effective in curbing future misbehavior, over the course of a school year your students will end up spending far less time in time out.
